name: DPM1-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ie)

clinicalPearls: DPM1 encodes the catalytic subunit of dolichol-phosphate mannosyltransferase (DPM synthase), which produces dolichol-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man).

Dol-P-Man is the shared mannose donor for four pathways, N-glycosylation, protein O-mannosylation (notably of alpha-dystroglycan), C-mannosylation and GPI-anchor synthesis, so DPM1-CDG uniquely bridges the CDGs and the dystroglycanopathies.
Clinically it presents with severe developmental delay, early epileptic encephalopathy, central hypotonia and acquired microcephaly.
Because O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan is impaired, patients show a muscular dystrophy phenotype with elevated creatine kinase, a clue that separates DPM1 from purely N-glycosylation CDGs.
Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin shows a type I pattern; assessment of alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation on muscle biopsy is complementary.
DPM synthase is a multi-subunit complex, so the allelic disorders DPM2-CDG and DPM3-CDG give overlapping CDG-dystroglycanopathy pictures.
Optic atrophy with visual failure is a recognised feature.
reference.pathophysiology: DPM1-CDG is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in DPM1, the gene encoding the catalytic subunit of dolichol-phosphate mannosyltransferase (DPM synthase). This endoplasmic reticulum enzyme transfers mannose from GDP-mannose onto dolichol phosphate to generate dolichol-phosphate-mannose, the obligatory mannose donor for the luminal steps of N-linked glycan assembly, for protein O-mannosylation (notably of alpha-dystroglycan), for C-mannosylation of tryptophan residues and for glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis. Because a single defective donor cripples several glycosylation pathways at once, DPM1-CDG combines the multisystem features of a type I CDG with a secondary dystroglycanopathy; deficient alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation disrupts its binding to extracellular-matrix ligands, producing muscle membrane instability, a muscular dystrophy phenotype with raised creatine kinase, while the accompanying N-glycan and GPI-anchor deficits drive a severe neurodevelopmental disorder.
additionalDifferentials: DPM2-CDG and DPM3-CDG, the other DPM synthase subunit defects and closest siblings
MPDU1-CDG and DOLK-CDG, disorders of Dol-P-Man utilisation with overlapping dystroglycanopathy features
Primary alpha-dystroglycanopathies (POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, FKTN, FKRP) across the muscle-eye-brain and Walker-Warburg spectrum
PMM2-CDG (CDG-Ia), the prototypic type I CDG
Congenital muscular dystrophies presenting with raised creatine kinase
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing / carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (type I pattern)
Serum creatine kinase, which is persistently elevated
Molecular testing or exome sequencing for biallelic DPM1 variants
Muscle biopsy with alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation immunostaining
EEG and MRI brain for structural, migrational and atrophic changes
Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins, given the shared donor pathway
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory muscle involvement
Markedly elevated creatine kinase with cardiac involvement or cardiomyopathy
Feeding failure with failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: The disorder is generally severe, with significant neurodevelopmental impairment and reduced survival, although severity varies with the degree of residual enzyme activity.
pitfalls: Missing the dystroglycanopathy and muscle component and classifying it as a pure N-glycosylation CDG.
Attributing an elevated creatine kinase to seizures or trauma rather than primary muscle disease.
Being falsely reassured by a normal-appearing transferrin pattern, so that genotyping and muscle studies are still required.
Overlooking cardiac surveillance despite the dystroglycanopathy overlap.

management: No disease-specific or curative therapy exists, so management is entirely supportive and multidisciplinary
Control the early epileptic encephalopathy with antiseizure medication and manage central hypotonia with physiotherapy and posture and seating support
Provide nutritional support with safe-feeding measures, using nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding where swallowing is unsafe
Offer developmental, occupational and speech therapy for the severe neurodevelopmental impairment and the associated muscular dystrophy phenotype
Monitor with serial EEG, creatine kinase and neuroimaging, and arrange ophthalmological surveillance for optic atrophy
Coordinate care across metabolic medicine, paediatric neurology, ophthalmology and rehabilitation
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive condition, with carrier testing and prenatal counselling for the family
